In the last section, for the graphs considered, we have seen that ejection seems to account for only a small part of the full scattering; this may be a consequence of the short range of the interaction we considered. 5 Conclusion Our systematic approach to studying two-particle scattering on graphs lays the groundwork for further development in several directions. In a more practical point of view, we can apply these new tools to different physical systems; the quantum-walk Hamiltonian of a particle on a graph is analogous to the tight-binding model in condensed matter physics, and our results could be applied to studying properties of electron transport in more general lattices, such as the hexagonal lattice of graphene; in optics, for example, we could apply quantum walk with the Hubbard interaction on specified vertices as a toy model to study photons interacting with a quantum dot network — we found strong similarities of scattering properties of simple families of graphs and the optical systems considered in [2, 3, 20]. On the other hand, we believe these results can shed new light on studying new graph theoretical properties in general; for example, some frequently studied properties in general single-particle walks are hitting times — the average time it takes for a particle to traverse between two given vertices — and mixing times — the average time it takes for the distribution to become stationary. We can ask similar questions in two-particle quantum walks: • Two-particle hitting times: What is the average time it takes for a particle to traverse a given graph when a second particle is in some bound state? What is the average time it takes for two particles initialized in some inner vertex to escape the graph? Some of our results in section 4.2 are similar to infinite hitting times discussed in [23]. • Two-particle mixing times: How long does it take for the bound particle to change to a different bound state in an inelastic scattering process? In opposition to the dynamics on finite graphs, scattering on graphs with rails is not periodic; it is possible to define asymptotic mixing times. In the perspective of quantum computation, we can explore new possible gadgets for quantum algorithms based on graphs, or more generally, quantum tasks. The graphs described in section 4.2 already exhibit many new properties that could be interesting: We can describe how the presence of a bound state on part of a graph can affect the trajectory of another particle traversing it. The graph AC(4) allows for a conditional momentum filter, a gadget that allows only a small range of the momentum wavepacket to be transmitted, depending on the energy of the evanescent bound particle present on the graph. In addition, by considering confined bound states, the same graph can serve as a kind of transistor, making a particle perfectly transmit or reflect through the graph depending on the presence of the bound particle. Also, even though we do not expect it is possible to construct a finite-sized graph which implements a perfect CPhase gate between two traveling particles [24], it is still open whether it is possible to intermediate an entangling gate using bound states; we leave this as an interesting open question. In the perspective of complexity theory, we opened the way to answer some open questions: since multi-particle interacting quantum walks are universal for quantum computing [4, 7], can a restricted form of quantum walks have intermediate computational power? 1. No interaction: In analogy to the boson-sampling model [1], are quantum walks with noninteracting bosons hard to simulate classically? Expanding the results in [9], can we show that quantum walks with non-interacting fermions are classically simulable?

statement: 2. Restricting momentum: Are quantum walks where all particles have the same initial momentum universal for quantum computing? In the original construction it is necessary to have particles with two different momenta interacting. 3. Restricting gadgets: Is there a restricted set of gadgets which makes quantum walks nonuniversal? In the original construction, the gadget which implements the Hadamard gate has maximal degree 4, therefore restricting the graph’s maximum degree to 3 could render quantum walks non-universal. 4. Bound states as resources: Given a non-universal set of gadgets, can initializing the graph with some number of bound particles make it universal? We applied our method only to the Hubbard model, but the formalism is easily applicable to other multi-particle potentials.
